plans.title: Genesis 1–4 in seven days
plans.description: Seven short devotionals. Each starts with a story, lays out the passage, shows what is worth discovering in it, and ends with something you can take into your day. The myth cards and insights are listed at the end for anyone who wants the sources.

days.title: Day 1: The first week
days.summary: A poem about a world made ready, looked at with delight, and ended in rest.

story.title: The room
text: Marta has six evenings before the baby comes, and the spare room is empty. On the first evening she opens the curtains and lets the light in. She stands in the doorway and looks. On the second she puts up the walls and the ceiling. On the third she lays the floor and brings in a plant. Each evening she says what she is about to do, does it, steps back and looks at it. Each evening the same quiet thought: good.
On the fourth evening she hangs a lamp. On the fifth she puts a bird mobile above the cot, and on the sixth she brings the cot in. Then she goes to fetch the one who will live there.
On the seventh evening there is nothing left to do. She sits in the finished room, and she does not leave.
Someone once wrote a poem about the whole world in exactly that rhythm. It is the first page of the Bible.
Read Genesis 1:1–2:3 aloud first, about five minutes. It was written for the ear. Then look at its shape.
bullets: Days 1–3 make the spaces: light and dark; sky and sea; land and plants.
Days 4–6 fill them: the lights in the sky; birds and fish; land animals and people.
Day 7 rests.
Every day follows one refrain: ‘God said… and it was so… God saw that it was good… there was evening and there was morning.’

The first line has seven Hebrew words and the second has fourteen. The description of the seventh day has thirty-five. Whether the writer planned the counting is an open question, but the poem is built around seven.

discoveries.heading: The world is looked at before it is used
text: Six times God speaks, and then stops to look. In the poem, delight comes first. Now watch where the refrain bends. Day 3 says ‘good’ twice, and the sixth day ends with ‘very good’. Day 2 does not say it at all, and nobody knows why. Let the silence stay open.

discoveries.heading: A house made ready
text: The poem shapes spaces before it puts anyone in them: light, then lights; sky and sea, then birds and fish; land, then animals and people. Many scholars read this as a literary frame, which is one reason they do not read the days as a timetable. Others read them as literal days or as ages, and all of those readings use the same pairing.

discoveries.heading: The lamps
text: The sun and moon are never named. They are ‘the greater light’ and ‘the lesser light’, hung in the sky to give light and mark the times. In the world around, these were gods with names, such as Shamash and Sin in Mesopotamia. Many readers hear a quiet freedom here: the biggest things in the sky are lamps. That the unnamed lights are a deliberate choice is an interpretation, since the Hebrew words for sun and moon exist.

discoveries.heading: The last one in the room
text: Every human, male and female, is made in God’s image. In Egypt and Mesopotamia, that title belonged to the king, who ruled for the god. Here it is given to everyone, and it is the first thing said about people, before they have done anything. (God’s ‘Let us make’ in 1:26 has been read as the Trinity, as God addressing the heavenly court, or as a king deliberating with himself. The text does not say who is addressed.)

discoveries.heading: A week that ends in rest
text: The seventh day has no ‘evening and morning’, and nothing is made on it. After six days of making, the climax of the week is a day with no work in it.

bullets: Look before you use. Today, take one ordinary thing, such as a cup, a window or a person, and say ‘good’ before you use it.
Name a lamp. What do you treat as huge that might be a lamp: a deadline, a number, an opinion of you?
Dignity first. Before you judge or help someone today, remember what the poem says about them.
Keep one open hour this week with nothing to produce.
questions: Where have you been given something before you did anything?

days.quickCheck: If you retell the days from memory, birds belong to Day 5 with the sea creatures, not to Day 6.

days.title: Day 2: The garden
days.summary: A close-up on one man, one garden, one job and one limit.

story.title: The keys
text: Tomás has just been handed the keys to an allotment. The old owner walks him along the rows. ‘Water it in the evening. Look after it. Eat whatever you like, beans, tomatoes, all of it. Only that one bed is not mine to give away, so leave it alone.’

Tomás has been given a job, a place, and a great deal of freedom, and only one limit. He stands at the gate with the keys in his hand and notices something odd: he is not thinking about the limit at all. He is thinking that someone trusted him with this.
Read Genesis 2:4–17. Chapter 2 tells the story again, from close up. You will notice that something has changed.
bullets: 2:4–7: the earth is dry, and the LORD God forms the human from the soil and breathes into his nose.
2:8–14: God plants a garden and four rivers flow from it.
2:15: the man is put in the garden ‘to work it and keep it’.
2:16–17: he may eat from every tree, except one.

discoveries.heading: Two ways of telling creation
text: In chapter 1 the name is Elohim. Here it is the LORD God (YHWH Elohim). In chapter 1 the humans come last. Here the man comes first, then the trees, the animals and the woman. The style changes from a patterned liturgy to a close-up story.

Notice also the mood. In chapter 1 everything is ‘good’ and finished. Chapter 2 holds the first thing God calls ‘not good’, which you will meet tomorrow. One way to read the difference is by what each chapter is for: chapter 1 shows creation as a finished order, and chapter 2 tells it as a story about a person, driven by a lack. On that reading the two chapters do not contradict each other, because they do different jobs.

Scholars explain the doubling in other ways too. Source critics see two sources (Priestly and Yahwist). Others see one author or editor, with 2:4 as the heading of a new section and chapter 2 as a zoom-in. These readings do not exclude each other, and all agree that the two units say different things in different ways. It is good to know which voice is speaking, and what it is doing.

discoveries.heading: Earthling
text: The first person is called adam, which sounds like adamah, ‘soil’. English hides the pun, but Hebrew listeners heard it: the human is an earthling, formed from the ground he will look after.

discoveries.heading: A job before anything goes wrong
text: The man is put in the garden ‘to work it and keep it’ (2:15). This is before the story has any trouble in it, which means that work belongs to the good beginning. What changes in chapter 3 is the ground and the kind of work, with toil, thorns and sweat. The same two verbs, ‘work’ and ‘keep’, appear together later for the duties of the Levites at the tent of meeting (Numbers 3:7–8). That is one reason many scholars read the garden as a first sanctuary and the man as a priest-gardener. It is a widely held proposal that others question.

discoveries.heading: Generosity first
text: The command begins with a wide yes: ‘You may freely eat of every tree’. The limit comes second and is one tree. Notice also that it is given before the woman exists. Keep that in mind for Day 4.

bullets: Think of what you have been trusted with: a home, a team, a garden, a child. Say thank you for it today, in words.
Notice your work today as something given, not only as a burden. Where is there still something good in it?
Where have you treated a single limit as if it were the whole story?
questions: The man is given a job and a limit before anything else. What does each one say about how God sees him?

days.quickCheck: The word in Genesis is ‘garden’ (gan). ‘Paradise’ comes from an Old Iranian word for a walled park that reached the Bible through the Greek translation. And work comes before the curse, not after it.

days.title: Day 3: Two become one
days.summary: The first thing God calls ‘not good’, and a poem of recognition.

story.title: The empty table
text: Jonas has moved to a new city for work. The flat is clean, the job is good, the fridge is full. On the first Sunday he sets the table for one and eats looking at the wall. Nothing is wrong. And he notices that, with everything in order, one thing is missing, and it is not a thing.

A week later a neighbour knocks to borrow a ladder, and they talk for an hour on the landing. It is not a rescue. It is just the first time in the city that someone has looked at him as if he were already known.
Read Genesis 2:18–25. After seven ‘goods’ in chapter 1, the first ‘not good’ is here.
bullets: 2:18: ‘It is not good that the man should be alone.’
2:19–20: the animals are brought to the man, and he names them, but no partner is found.
2:21–22: God makes a deep sleep fall on the man, and builds a woman from ‘one of his tselot’.
2:23: the man’s poem.
2:24–25: leaving, joining, and being naked without shame.

discoveries.heading: The first ‘not good’
text: The problem the story names is not that the man is a poor worker. It is that he is alone. God’s response is to look for a match, and he first brings the animals. The naming shows that none of them is a partner.

discoveries.heading: A help ‘in front of him’
text: God says he will make an ezer kenegdo, ‘a help corresponding to him’. ‘Helper’ is a fair translation, but the word does not mean ‘assistant’. In the Old Testament it is often used of God as Israel’s help (for example Psalm 121:1–2; Deuteronomy 33:26, 29), so being the helper does not mean being lower. The second word adds correspondence, like to like. Scholars differ on how much to build on it, and the modest reading is the one that holds on all sides: the text gives no basis for treating the woman as lesser.

discoveries.heading: Made from his side
text: The Hebrew word tsela elsewhere nearly always means ‘side’, as in the sides of the ark or a hillside, so many translators read ‘one of his sides’. The Latin costa (‘rib’) set the English tradition, and whether ‘rib’ is still possible here is argued. The point of the story is clear either way: she is made from the same stuff as the man, not from dust like the animals. That is kinship, not rank.

discoveries.heading: A poem of recognition
text: The man’s first words are a poem: ‘This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.’ ‘At last’ is the sound of relief. Then comes a pun on sound: she shall be called ishah (woman) because she was taken from ish (man). The astonishment is real, but the pun is ish and ishah. A pun can make a point memorable, but it cannot prove one.

discoveries.heading: Naked, and not ashamed
text: The scene ends with the pair ‘naked and not ashamed’. The word for naked, arummim, sounds like arum, ‘crafty’, which opens the next chapter. Hold on to that word, because it is where the serpent will aim tomorrow.

bullets: Who in your life is not a helper in the sense of ‘useful’, but someone who looks at you as already known? Tell them today.
If you are the one alone, say so to someone. The story says that being alone is the first thing that is not good.
Pay attention to how you describe the people close to you. Do you describe them as assistants or as people ‘in front of’ you?
questions: God names the first thing that is ‘not good’. What is it, and who solves it?

days.quickCheck: ‘Wow-man’ is an English sound-joke and is not in the Hebrew. ‘Life-saver’ is a gloss, not a translation of ezer. And a Hebrew word-study should never be the only support for how two people share a life.

days.title: Day 4: A question that shrinks
days.summary: A conversation in which a generous rule is bent a little at a time.

story.title: The blue tin
text: Lena’s mother says: ‘Take anything from the kitchen. Just not the biscuits in the blue tin, I am saving those for Sunday.’ Later, Lena’s friend asks, quite casually: ‘Really? Your mum said you can’t have anything to eat?’
Lena says: ‘No, only the blue tin.’ Then, because the friend looks doubtful: ‘We’re not even allowed to touch it.’ Her mother never said that, but it feels safer.
Her friend shrugs. ‘It’s not like she would find out.’ Lena looks at the kitchen. For the first time she sees only one thing in it.
Read Genesis 3:1–7. It is a short conversation with a quick end, so slow down.
bullets: 3:1: the serpent’s question.
3:2–3: the woman’s answer.
3:4–5: the serpent’s reply.
3:6: she sees, takes and eats, and gives to her husband, who is ‘with her’ (immah).
3:7: their eyes are opened, they know they are naked, and they sew coverings.

discoveries.heading: A creature with a pun
text: The serpent is ‘more crafty (arum) than any other wild animal that the LORD God had made’: it is one of the animals. The word arum sounds like arummim, ‘naked’, from 2:25. One sound, two senses: exposed and clever. The serpent’s skill is in turning openness into fear. The later Christian reading that the serpent is Satan (for example Revelation 12:9) is old and widely held, but it is a reading and not in this chapter.

discoveries.heading: Listen to the first question
text: ‘Did God really say, You shall not eat from any tree in the garden?’ Compare it with what God said in 2:16–17, which was a wide yes and one exception. The question leaves out the generosity and makes the limit the whole story. This is how a rule shrinks: not by a lie, but by a change of emphasis.

discoveries.heading: A little extra
text: The woman’s answer is mostly accurate, but she adds ‘neither shall you touch it’. God’s command did not contain it, and it was given before she existed. The text does not say who added the words or why. Genesis Rabbah treats it as a fault, while Rashi and Avot de-Rabbi Natan say that Adam added it as a protective ‘fence’. The reading that Eve added it out of care has no strong ancient support. Whichever you choose, a protective rule that is quoted as if God had said it can begin to take the place of the reason.

discoveries.heading: The fruit, and the one who was with her
text: Genesis never names the fruit. It says only ‘the fruit of the tree’. The text says the man was ‘with her’. Whether he was at the conversation is argued: the serpent’s ‘you’ in verses 1–5 is plural, which some take as a sign that he was there, while others say that ‘with her’ does not prove presence. The words ‘lead’ and ‘headship’ appear nowhere in these verses. The passage cannot settle the argument between complementarian and egalitarian readings, and it should not be used as a weapon in it.

discoveries.heading: Eyes opened
text: Both eat. Both discover they are naked. Both sew coverings. The openness that was safety has turned into shame, and that is the serpent’s achievement.

bullets: Listen this week for the question that shrinks: ‘Did they really say…?’ ‘Are you really not allowed…?’ Notice what it leaves out.
Think of a rule you quote that is a little longer than the original. Does it still serve its purpose, or has it replaced the reason?
When you remember a story, check one small detail against the source. It takes two minutes and earns trust.
questions: Read the serpent’s first question slowly. What does it change about what God said?

days.quickCheck: The fruit is never named, and the apple is a later European picture. The claim that the Hebrew word for ‘male’ (zakar) means ‘the one who remembers’ fails whatever the etymology, since a word’s meaning comes from its use and not from shared consonants.
days.safeguard: Genesis 3 is often used to say who should lead, or who is to blame. If you have been told that this story makes you responsible for another person’s behaviour, or that you must submit, the text does not say so.

days.title: Day 5: Questions before verdicts
days.summary: A court that begins with questions, and a closing scene in which God clothes the people who failed.

story.title: Behind the sofa
text: The vase is in pieces on the floor, and eight-year-old Noor is behind the sofa when she hears the key in the door. Her father comes in, sees the mess and, to her surprise, does not shout. He says: ‘Noor, where are you?’

She comes out. ‘Did you break it?’ ‘It was the dog.’ The dog, hearing his name, wags his tail. Her father almost smiles. He says nothing about punishment yet. He kneels and starts to pick up the pieces, and he tells her to find her slippers so she will not cut her feet.
Read Genesis 3:8–24. It is the longest scene so far, so read it in four parts.
bullets: 3:8–13: God walks in the garden, and asks three questions.
3:14–15: the verdict on the serpent.
3:16–19: the consequences for the woman and the man.
3:20–24: the naming of Eve, the garments of skin, and the exit.

discoveries.heading: A walk, and a question
text: They hear God ‘walking’ in the garden. The same verb is used for God’s presence among his people in Leviticus 26:12. The man hides. God’s first words are not an accusation but a question: ‘Where are you?’ Then ‘Who told you that you were naked?’ and ‘What is this that you have done?’

discoveries.heading: A court that runs backwards
text: God asks the man first (3:9), then the woman (3:13), and the serpent is not questioned at all. Then the sentences run in the order of the offence: serpent, woman, man. The scene is built as a court, with inquiry from the end of the chain to its start, and then judgment. Everyone points to someone else: the man to the woman ‘whom you gave me’, the woman to the serpent. Each is partly true, and each avoids the question. The scene is more useful as a mirror than as a ruling on who is to blame, and it gives no support for ranking blame between the sexes.

discoveries.heading: Who is called cursed
text: Listen for the word ‘cursed’ (arur). God says it to the serpent (3:14) and to the ground ‘because of you’ (3:17). He does not say it to the woman or the man. They receive consequences: pain, toil, and a return to dust. Hardship here is a consequence, and it is not the same thing as a curse on the person.

discoveries.heading: Verse 15
text: God tells the serpent that there will be enmity between its seed and the woman’s seed: ‘he shall strike your head, and you shall strike his heel.’ ‘Seed’ is a collective noun, and no one is named. The first surviving Christian reading that links the verse to Christ is Irenaeus (about 180). Jewish readings are more varied than ‘non-messianic’: the Palestinian Targums speak of healing in the days of the Messiah, and the verse is otherwise read morally and collectively. Anyone who has been wronged can hear in it that evil gets a verdict and that harm is not the last word, and you can hold that without claiming that the verse names Jesus.

discoveries.heading: Verse 16
text: To the woman: ‘your desire (teshuqah) shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you.’ This is a hard verse and its meaning is argued. It announces a consequence of a broken world and gives no instruction. You will meet the same rare word teshuqah tomorrow, in a different place.

discoveries.heading: Clothes, and a door
text: The scene closes with an act: ‘The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them.’ The verse mentions no altar, blood or atonement. Many Christians have seen a pointer to sacrifice and to Christ’s covering of sin, and that is a long and respected reception. What the verse says is that God clothes people who have just failed him. Then he sends them out, with cherubim on the east side.

bullets: Notice the sentence you reach for when asked ‘What happened?’ Is it a fact or a pointer to someone else?
When someone you care for has done wrong, try asking before you judge. Let them answer.
Think of the last time someone covered you when you failed. Thank them.
questions: God asks before he sentences. Which of the questions would be hardest for you to answer?

days.quickCheck: Neither the man nor the woman is called cursed. The word ‘fall’ is not in the chapter, and Augustine, the Orthodox churches and rabbinic Judaism read it in different ways. The skins are not described as a sacrifice.
days.safeguard: Verses like 3:16 have been used to excuse control and harm in relationships. The text announces a consequence of a broken world and gives no command to dominate or to submit to abuse.

days.title: Day 6: Before the deed
days.summary: God speaks to Cain before anything has happened, and the choice is still open.

story.title: The stairs
text: At the school prize evening, Sam’s friend Joe is called to the stage for the project they both worked on. Sam’s name is not called. He claps, and then he walks out and sits on the stairs, hot in the face.

His teacher, Mrs Adler, finds him. She does not say ‘it’s not fair’ and she does not say ‘calm down’. She sits two steps below him and says: ‘You look angry. That’s allowed. But I’d like you to think before you go back in, because the next thing you do is yours.’
Sam says nothing. But he does not go back in yet.
Read Genesis 4:1–16. The story moves fast, so look for what God says.
bullets: 4:1–2: two births, and two names.
4:3–5: two offerings, and Cain’s anger.
4:6–7: God speaks to Cain.
4:8–10: the killing, and God’s question.
4:11–16: the sentence, the sign, and Cain’s exit.

discoveries.heading: Two names
text: Eve says ‘I have gotten (qanithi) a man…’, and the sound-play with Qayin (Cain) is certain. ‘Treasure’ is not a standard gloss, and the usual renderings are ‘acquired one’ or ‘possession’. Many scholars also connect qayin with a word for ‘smith’ (compare Tubal-Cain in 4:22). The second son is Hevel, Abel, the word Ecclesiastes uses for life’s breath-like brevity. A Hebrew listener would hear that his part will be short. The text does not say why Eve chose the name.

discoveries.heading: Two offerings, no reason given
text: Cain brings ‘some of the fruits of the soil’. Abel brings ‘the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions’. Those two words appear only for Abel. Hebrews 11:4 reads his offering as an act of faith, which is the strongest reading, but it is still an inference. The text gives no reason for God’s response.

discoveries.heading: God speaks first
text: When Cain is angry, God does not wait. He asks, ‘Why are you angry?’ and says: ‘If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire (teshuqah) is for you, but you must rule (mashal) over it.’ These are the same two rare words as in 3:16. Both verses describe what goes wrong in a broken world, and neither is an instruction. 4:7 ends with a call to master sin, which shows that a description is not a destiny. Between the feeling and the act, the story places a pause, and puts the choice there.

discoveries.heading: The second question
text: After the killing, God asks again: ‘Where is Abel your brother?’ It echoes ‘Where are you?’ in chapter 3. The first question was about a person’s relation to God, the second about relations with others. Cain answers with a question, ‘Am I my brother’s keeper?’, using the same verb (shamar) that the man was given for the garden. Abel’s blood (the Hebrew is plural, ‘bloods’) cries from the ground, and the ground the first man was made from will no longer yield for Cain.

discoveries.heading: Mercy that is not repentance
text: The text records no confession from Cain. His word avon in 4:13 can mean ‘guilt’ or ‘punishment’, and most translations read ‘my punishment is more than I can bear’. His fear is that he will be killed. God puts a sign (ot) on him ‘so that no one who found him would kill him’. Genesis does not say what the sign was, and its purpose is protection. Nothing in the text links it to skin colour or a people.

bullets: Name your early warnings: what happens in your body or your thoughts before anger turns into action? Write down two.
When you feel the pause, treat it as a gift, as in the story. Take a minute before you answer.
Both of God’s questions are worth asking: ‘Where are you?’ and ‘Where is your brother?’ Which have you been avoiding?
questions: God speaks to Cain before he acts. What exactly does God say to him, and what is left for Cain to decide?

days.quickCheck: ‘Treasure’ is not a standard rendering of Cain. The sign on Cain is never described and has nothing to do with skin colour. And God’s mercy to Cain does not remove his consequences, nor does it say that anyone must reconcile with a person who has not changed.
days.safeguard: God’s mercy to Cain does not tell anyone to forgive or reconcile with a person who has harmed them and has not changed.

days.title: Day 7: Two families
days.summary: Two lines, one name, and a choice that repeats in every generation.

story.title: The same name
text: Two cousins are named after the same grandfather. One grows up in a house where the rule is ‘never let anyone hurt us without paying for it’. At his own wedding he makes a speech about it, and everyone laughs a little too loudly.
The other grows up in a house where the grandmother says, whenever a baby is born, ‘this one will bring us some relief’. When his own son is born he says it too, and means it.
Same name, same family, two directions.
Read Genesis 4:17–26, and then 5:28–29 for comparison.
bullets: 4:17–22: Cain’s line, seven generations: a city, herds, music and metalwork.
4:23–24: Lamech’s song.
4:25–26: Seth is born, and then Enosh, and people begin to call on the name of the LORD.
5:28–29: another Lamech, in Seth’s line, names his son Noah.

discoveries.heading: A family that makes things
text: Cain builds a city. Jabal keeps herds, Jubal plays the lyre and the pipe, and Tubal-Cain forges tools of bronze and iron. Nothing in the text condemns these arts. The line ends with Lamech, who takes two wives and sings a poem to them.

discoveries.heading: Lamech’s song
text: ‘I have killed a man for wounding me… If Cain is avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy-sevenfold.’ His poem sets his own vengeance against Cain’s protection and multiplies it. Two details are open. The first verb (ki haragti) can be read ‘I have killed’ or ‘I would kill (if)’, and the text never says whom he killed. Many readers call the poem a ‘Song of the Sword’ and link it to Tubal-Cain’s metalwork. The text gives no sign of fear and no sign that he keeps it private: his audience inside the story is his wives. Violence that escalates and then boasts is recognisable anywhere, and Jesus reverses the number when Peter asks how often to forgive: not seven times but seventy-seven (Matthew 18:21–22).

discoveries.heading: The other Lamech
text: Now read chapter 5. The names in Seth’s line sound like those in Cain’s: Enoch, Jared and Irad, Mahalalel and Mehujael, Methuselah and Methushael, and Lamech again. Cain’s line has seven generations and Seth’s has ten. Source critics explain the likeness as two versions of one list, and others read it as a deliberate contrast. Both keep the contrast. This Lamech names his son Noah in hope: ‘this one shall bring us relief from our work’.

discoveries.heading: How it ends
text: Chapter 4 does not end with the city or the sword, but with a birth and a beginning: ‘At that time people began to call on the name of the LORD.’ Two families are set side by side. One builds cities and arts and weapons, and one calls on the LORD. The choice repeats in each generation, and Noah is the turn.

bullets: Look at what you have inherited: sayings, habits, stories that explain how a family answers harm. Which ones would you pass on, and which would you stop?
Choose one phrase from the second family to say this week. For example, ‘this one will bring us relief’.
Notice when something you make or build is used as a weapon, and decide which line you are in.
questions: Who do the last verses say begins to ‘call on the name of the LORD’, and why might the writer end here?

days.quickCheck: The claim that Lamech boasts only in private is not in the text, and it is one reading of an unclear verb.
days.finish: Take the quiz to review the week.

plans.title: Small group: four evenings
plans.description: Four evenings for a small group. Each starts with a story read aloud, lays out the passage, shows the discoveries to explore together, and ends with questions that lead into the week. The leader does not need to be an expert. The myth cards and insights are listed at the end for anyone who wants the sources.

days.title: Evening 1: Order and dignity
days.summary: A poem about a world made ready, and a dignity given to every person.

story.title: The room (read aloud, 5 minutes)
text: Marta has six evenings before the baby comes, and the spare room is empty. Each evening she does one thing: the light, the walls, the floor, the lamp, the mobile, the cot. Each evening she steps back, looks, and thinks: good. On the seventh evening there is nothing left to do, and she sits in the finished room.
Ask: what did you grow up hearing about Genesis 1? Write the answers down without comment, and return to them at the end.
Read Genesis 1:1–2:3 aloud, with a different reader for each day (10 minutes). It was written to be heard.
bullets: Days 1–3 make the spaces. Days 4–6 fill them. Day 7 rests.
The refrain: ‘God said… it was so… God saw that it was good… evening and morning.’
Seven Hebrew words in 1:1, fourteen in 1:2, thirty-five for the seventh day. Whether the counting was planned is an inference.

discoveries.heading: Where does the pattern bend? (10 minutes)
text: In the Hebrew, Day 2 never says ‘good’, Day 3 says it twice and Day 6 says ‘very good’. Ask the group what they think the poem does with the variation, and leave it open: why Day 2 is silent is an old guess and not settled. Many scholars read the pairing of Days 1–3 and 4–6 as a literary frame, others read literal days or ages, and all of them use the same pairing, so the group does not need to settle that tonight.

discoveries.heading: What is missing? (10 minutes)
text: The sun and moon are never named. In Mesopotamia they were gods. Many readers hear a quiet freedom in that: the neighbours’ powers are lamps in God’s creation. This is an interpretation, so present it as one. Ask what the group treats as a ‘greater light’ today.

discoveries.heading: Who is made in the image? (10 minutes)
text: In Egypt and Mesopotamia the king was the image of the god. Here every human, male and female, is. Chapter 2 tells the story again in another voice, so say now that there are two units and that they differ. Ask what it means to meet someone as an image of God this week.

bullets: This week, say ‘good’ about one ordinary thing before you use it.
Choose one person you tend to rank, and treat them as an image of God for a day.
Keep one open hour with nothing to produce.
questions: What in the text surprised you tonight?
What does ‘image of God’ for every person change in how you meet someone this week?

days.quickCheck: Birds are on Day 5, with the sea creatures. A retelling from memory often moves them to Day 6.

days.title: Evening 2: Two people, one garden
days.summary: A job, a limit, and a person made to be met.
days.leaderNote: This evening touches on how Genesis 2–3 is used in marriages. Read the care note in the app first and be ready to point people to the help page. Do not ask anyone to share personal stories about their own relationship.

story.title: The keys (read aloud, 3 minutes)
text: Tomás has been handed the keys to an allotment. The old owner says: ‘Water it in the evening and look after it. Eat whatever you like. Only that one bed is not mine to give away.’ Tomás stands at the gate and notices he is not thinking about the one bed at all. He is thinking that someone trusted him with this.
Ask: what is the first thing you have been trusted with, in your life?
Read Genesis 2:4–25 aloud (10 minutes).
bullets: 2:4–17: the human from the soil, the garden, the job and the limit.
2:18–20: the first ‘not good’, and the animals.
2:21–25: the woman, the man’s poem, and ‘naked and not ashamed’.

discoveries.heading: A job before anything goes wrong (10 minutes)
text: The man is put in the garden ‘to work it and keep it’ (2:15) before there is any trouble in the story, so work is part of the good beginning. The same two verbs describe the Levites’ duties, so many scholars see the garden as a first sanctuary (a proposal that others question). Ask what it would mean to think of work as attention to God.

discoveries.heading: The first ‘not good’ (10 minutes)
text: The problem is not that the man is incomplete as a worker. It is that he is alone. Ask what the group makes of the fact that the first ‘not good’ in the Bible is about loneliness.

discoveries.heading: Words that were heard ‘from the Hebrew’ (15 minutes)
text: Take the claims the group heard against the text, one at a time. ‘Helper’ (ezer) is not a mistranslation, and it is often used of God, so it does not mean ‘lesser’. ‘Life-saver’ is a gloss. ‘Rib’ is tsela, which usually means ‘side’, and the point is that she is made from the same stuff as the man. ‘Wow-man’ is an English joke, and the Hebrew pun is ish and ishah. And the idea that the word for ‘male’ (zakar) makes the man ‘the one who remembers’ fails whatever the etymology, because a word’s meaning comes from use and not from shared consonants. The point is not to win arguments, but that a word-study should never be the only support for how two people share a life.

bullets: Say thank you this week for something you have been entrusted with.
Ask someone close to you how they would like to be known and helped, instead of assuming.
When you hear ‘the Hebrew really means…’ this week, ask where it comes from.
questions: Which claim about men and women have you heard ‘from the Hebrew’? What does the text itself say, and what was added?
What would change if work were part of the good beginning and not part of the curse?

days.quickCheck: The Hebrew word in Genesis is ‘garden’ (gan). ‘Paradise’ is a later word that reached the Bible through the Greek translation.

days.title: Evening 3: Blame and mercy
days.summary: A conversation, a court of questions, and a scene of clothing.
days.leaderNote: Do not use this evening to assign blame between the sexes. The text gives no support for ranking blame, and it does not settle who should lead. If someone says that Genesis 3 means they must submit to a partner or take the blame for another person’s behaviour, say gently that the text does not say so, and point to the help page.

story.title: Behind the sofa (read aloud, 3 minutes)
text: The vase is in pieces, and eight-year-old Noor is hiding behind the sofa when she hears the key in the door. Her father comes in, sees the mess, and does not shout. He says: ‘Noor, where are you?’ She comes out. ‘Did you break it?’ ‘It was the dog.’ The dog wags his tail. Her father kneels and starts to pick up the pieces, and tells her to find her slippers so she will not cut her feet.
Ask: what do you picture when you hear ‘the Fall’? Write the answers down without comment.
Read Genesis 3 in three parts, by three readers (10 minutes).
bullets: 3:1–7: the conversation.
3:8–19: the questions and the verdicts.
3:20–24: the clothing and the exit.

discoveries.heading: A question that shrinks (10 minutes)
text: ‘Did God really say, You shall not eat from any tree?’ leaves out the generosity of 2:16–17 and makes the limit the whole story. The woman’s answer adds ‘neither shall you touch it’, which is not in God’s command. The text does not say who added it, and ancient readers split. Ask where a protective rule has taken the place of its reason.

discoveries.heading: What the story does not say (10 minutes)
text: No fruit is named. The serpent is a creature, ‘more crafty than any other wild animal’, and its identification with Satan comes later. The man is ‘with her’, and the text says nothing about him failing to lead. Neither the woman nor the man is called cursed: only the serpent and the ground. ‘Fall’ is not a word in the chapter. Each of these has a card in the app, so choose two or three depending on what the group raised in the opening.

discoveries.heading: The questions (10 minutes)
text: God asks before he sentences: ‘Where are you? Who told you that you were naked? What is this that you have done?’ The man points to the woman, and the woman to the serpent. Ask where we do this today.

discoveries.heading: The clothes (5 minutes)
text: God clothes the people who have just failed him (3:21). Many Christians have seen a pointer to sacrifice in the skins, which is a long and respected reception, but the verse says only that God clothed them. Verse 15 speaks of the woman’s ‘seed’ as a collective. It has been read as pointing to Christ since Irenaeus, and Jewish readers have read it morally and collectively. You can hold that evil gets a verdict without claiming the verse names Jesus.

bullets: When someone asks ‘What happened?’ this week, notice whether you answer with a fact or a pointer.
Ask before you judge, once, with someone you are tempted to blame.
Cover someone, quietly, who has failed.
questions: Each person in the story points to someone else. Where do we do this today?
What would it look like to answer God’s question ‘Where are you?’ honestly?

days.quickCheck: The apple is a later picture, and the fruit is never named.
days.safeguard: Verses from Genesis 3 are sometimes used to justify control in a relationship. The text announces consequences of a broken world and gives no command to dominate or to submit to abuse.

days.title: Evening 4: Anger, violence and a different line
days.summary: God warns before the deed. Two families answer in different ways.
days.leaderNote: Cain’s protection does not mean a victim must reconcile with an unrepentant person. Say so out loud if forgiveness comes up.

story.title: The stairs (read aloud, 3 minutes)
text: At a school prize evening, Sam’s friend is called to the stage for the project they both worked on. Sam’s name is not called. He claps, then walks out and sits on the stairs, hot in the face. His teacher finds him and sits two steps below. She says: ‘You look angry. That’s allowed. But the next thing you do is yours.’ Sam says nothing, but he does not go back in yet.
Ask: when did you last feel your anger rising, before you did anything? Do not ask for stories. Just let the question sit.
Read Genesis 4:1–16 aloud (10 minutes).
bullets: 4:1–7: the births, the offerings, Cain’s anger and God’s words.
4:8–16: the killing, God’s question, the sentence and the sign.
Afterwards, read 4:17–26 and then 5:28–29.

discoveries.heading: The warning (15 minutes)
text: God speaks to Cain before he acts: ‘Sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.’ The two rare words, desire and rule, are the same ones as in 3:16. What the pair means is argued, but both verses describe what goes wrong in a broken world, and 4:7 ends with a call to master sin. Description is not destiny. Ask what the early warnings are, and what in our lives asks ‘Why are you angry?’

discoveries.heading: Two questions (10 minutes)
text: After the killing God asks ‘Where is Abel your brother?’, which echoes ‘Where are you?’ in chapter 3. The first question is about a person’s relation to God, the second about relations with others. Ask which is easier to answer.

discoveries.heading: Mercy without repentance (10 minutes)
text: The text records no confession from Cain, and his word avon can mean ‘guilt’ or ‘punishment’. God still puts a sign on him so that no one will kill him. Genesis does not say what the sign was, and it has no link to skin colour. Ask where mercy without repentance troubles the group, and where it comforts. Say clearly that God’s mercy to Cain does not remove consequences, and that it does not tell anyone to reconcile with someone who has not changed.

discoveries.heading: Two Lamechs (10 minutes)
text: Cain’s line ends in a song of vengeance, ‘seventy-sevenfold’ (the first verb is open: ‘I have killed’ or ‘I would kill’), which Jesus reverses in Matthew 18:21–22. Seth’s line has a Lamech too, who names his son Noah in hope. Same name, another direction. End on 4:26: people began to call on the name of the LORD.

bullets: Name two early warnings of your own anger, and tell one person.
Choose one saying from your family that you would pass on, and one that you would stop.
Take one minute this week to stop before you answer.
questions: God warns Cain before the deed. What are the early warnings in your life?
Where does mercy without repentance trouble you, and where does it comfort you?

days.quickCheck: ‘Treasure’ is not a standard rendering of Cain’s name. The sign on Cain has no link to skin colour.
days.safeguard: God’s mercy to Cain does not tell anyone to forgive or reconcile with a person who has harmed them and has not changed.
days.finish: End with the quiz as a game, in teams.
